n: Paul’s journey to Rome begins. He and other prisoners were placed in the care of Julius, a centurion of an imperial regiment. The “we” shows Luke is traveling with Paul.

f.g: The Imperial Cohort — a unit with a title honoring the emperor.

n: They boarded a ship from Adramyttium, a port near Troas, planning to hug the coast of Asia. Aristarchus of Thessalonica came along as a loyal companion.
The next day they stopped at Sidon, and Julius kindly let Paul visit friends for care. Paul’s character won the trust of his guards.

f.g: Treated kindly.

n: Contrary winds forced them to sail on the sheltered side of Cyprus.

f.g: Sailed in the lee of Cyprus, sheltered from the wind.

n: Crossing the open sea along the coast of southern Asia Minor, they reached Myra in Lycia.

f.g: A major harbor for grain ships sailing between Egypt and Rome.

n: There Julius found an Alexandrian grain ship bound for Italy and transferred them to it.

f.g: Large grain freighters carried Egyptian wheat to feed Rome.

n: Progress was slow against the wind. They barely reached Cnidus, then turned south to shelter along Crete, past Cape Salmone.

f.g: The wind not allowing us to go on.

n: With difficulty they reached a harbor called Fair Havens on Crete’s south coast, near Lasea.

f.g: With difficulty.

n: Much time had passed, and the season for safe sailing was ending — the Day of Atonement fast (late September or October) was already past. Paul warned them.

f.g: The Day of Atonement; after mid-September Mediterranean sailing grew dangerous, and it largely stopped by November.
Warned, advised.

n: Paul predicted the voyage would bring disaster — loss of cargo, ship, and possibly lives. His warning came from experience and perhaps inspiration.

f.g: Cargo.

n: But the centurion trusted the ship’s captain and owner over Paul. Expert opinion was against the prisoner’s advice.

f.g: The pilot or captain.

n: Fair Havens was poorly suited for winter, so most wanted to push on to Phoenix, a better harbor farther west on Crete.

f.g: Suitable, convenient.
Phoenix, a harbor on Crete — not Phoenicia.

n: A gentle south wind gave them false confidence. They set sail, staying close to Crete’s shore.
Soon a violent northeaster swept down from the island — a storm sailors called Euroclydon.

f.g: A violent northeast wind; often called the “Euraquilo” or northeaster.
Stormy, violent.

n: The ship couldn’t face into the wind, so they gave up and let it be driven along.

f.g: Let the ship run before the wind.

n: Sheltered briefly behind the small island of Cauda, they struggled to haul in the ship’s lifeboat.

f.g: Cauda, a small island south of Crete.
The small dinghy usually towed behind.

n: They passed ropes under the hull to hold it together and, fearing the sandbars off Libya, lowered the sails and drifted.

f.g: Wrapping cables around the hull to keep it from breaking apart.
The Syrtis — dangerous shoals off North Africa.
Lowered the sail or gear.

n: Battered by the storm, the next day they began throwing cargo overboard.
On the third day they threw the ship’s gear overboard with their own hands.

f.g: The ship’s rigging and equipment.

n: For many days they saw neither sun nor stars — sailors’ only means of navigation — and the storm raged on. They gave up all hope of survival.
After they had gone long without food, Paul stood up among them. He gently reminded them they should have listened to him — not to gloat, but to give weight to what he was about to say.

f.g: Going without food — from seasickness, fear, and spoiled supplies.

n: Now take heart, he said: no one will lose their life — only the ship will be lost.
An angel of the God to whom Paul belonged and whom he served had stood beside him that night.

f.w: whose I am, and whom I serve

n: The angel said: Don’t be afraid — you must stand before Caesar, and God has granted you the lives of everyone sailing with you. Others were spared because of Paul’s faithfulness.

f.w: God hath given thee all them that sail with thee

n: So take courage — I trust God that it will happen just as I was told. Paul’s faith becomes an anchor for everyone else.
Still, they would run aground on an island.
On the fourteenth night, drifting across the Adriatic Sea, the sailors sensed they were nearing land.

f.g: The central Mediterranean between Greece, Italy, and Sicily — wider than today’s Adriatic Sea.

n: They took soundings and found the water getting shallower — 120 feet, then 90 feet.

f.g: Measured the depth with a weighted line.
A fathom is about six feet.

n: Afraid of hitting rocks, they dropped four anchors from the stern and prayed for daylight.

f.g: Literally “prayed for day to come.”

n: The sailors secretly lowered the lifeboat, pretending to set more anchors from the bow, but planning to abandon ship.

f.g: Under pretense.
The bow, front of the ship.

n: Paul warned the centurion and soldiers: unless these men stay aboard, you can’t be saved. God’s promise still required human cooperation — the sailors’ skill was needed.

f.w: Except these abide in the ship, ye cannot be saved
f.g: Divine promises often work together with human effort.

n: This time the soldiers listened. They cut the lifeboat’s ropes and let it drift away.
Before dawn, Paul urged everyone to eat — they had gone fourteen days in anxious near-fasting.

f.g: Take food, eat.

n: Eat for your strength, he said — not a hair of your heads will perish. They would need energy to reach shore.

f.w: there shall not an hair fall from the head of any of you

n: Paul took bread, thanked God in front of everyone, broke it, and began to eat. His calm, grateful example spoke louder than words.
Everyone was encouraged and ate too.
There were 276 people on board — a large grain ship carrying many passengers.
After eating, they lightened the ship further by throwing the wheat cargo overboard, so it would ride higher and get closer to shore.
At daylight they didn’t recognize the land, but they saw a bay with a beach and planned to run the ship ashore there.

f.g: A bay or inlet.

n: They cut away the anchors, untied the steering oars, raised the foresail, and headed for the beach.

f.g: Ropes that had lashed up the steering paddles.
Hoisted.

n: They struck a sandbar where currents met. The bow stuck fast while the pounding surf broke the stern apart.

f.w: a place where two seas met
f.g: A sandbar or reef between two currents; traditionally identified with St. Paul’s Bay, Malta.

n: The soldiers planned to kill the prisoners so none could escape — they would be punished if prisoners got away.

f.w: lest any of them should swim out

n: But the centurion, wanting to save Paul, stopped them. He ordered swimmers to jump overboard first and get to land.
The rest followed on planks and broken pieces of the ship — and every one of the 276 reached land safely, just as God had promised.

f.w: they escaped all safe to land
